title: Actual beta-blocker exposure before surgery
clarityIssues: The visit-to-operation interval is unstated; the task could mean an immediate operative-day instruction or a longer preparation plan.

cues.why: The presentation classifies the order as new initiation and supplies its purpose, doing the decisive reconciliation inference.

fairness: Omitting new operative-day beta blockade is the best offered plan. No confident clinical error identified in that narrow rule. Absence of current symptoms does not establish absence of a chronic cardiac indication, so the rationale for not reassessing earlier needs clearer indication history.
Standalone. As written, explicit cessation months ago followed by a familiar initiation rule is easy rather than two consequential inferences.
suggestions: Specify the decision time and relevant established indication history. Show neutral administration/dispensing observations rather than calling the order a first replacement dose.
Compare credible plans requiring actual exposure and indication to be interpreted; do not invent a dose or titration interval.

title: Warfarin interruption for colectomy
fairness: Temporary interruption without routine therapeutic bridging is the best offered plan for the represented AF history and major bowel resection. The operation and anticoagulant indication both matter.
The bridge is a credible perioperative error; continuing therapeutic warfarin misapplies a minor-procedure strategy. No competing best answer identified in this scope.
Standalone. The explanation appropriately separates therapeutic bridging from surgical VTE prophylaxis. Exact timing and high-risk exceptions are not tested.
suggestions: Retain the indication, relevant embolic history and procedure. Delete the sentence merely announcing that the surgeon is comparing instructions.

cues.why: The task repeats the interpretation that determines the answer.

Compare plausible prevention decisions with a genuine competing-risk inference, or seek explicit basic-safety acceptance. Do not conceal necessary bleeding findings.

title: Reassessing prophylaxis after hemostasis
clarityIssues: Specify VTE prevention in the task rather than only 'Which prevention change'.
Renal function 'unchanged from baseline' does not establish whether baseline renal function supports the proposed LMWH approach.

cues.why: This conclusion follows several redundant reassuring observations and supplies the principal inference.

cues.why: Treatment intensity without diagnosed VTE is a weak alternative, leaving add prophylaxis versus preserve an obsolete hold.

fairness: Adding prophylaxis is the likely best plan after the described recovery, but relevant baseline renal status and drug contraindications should be clear.

Chronology is coherent. Earlier feedback already teaches conditional mechanical prevention and reassessment, and this update announces that the condition has resolved. This is strongly scaffolded rather than independent two-step reasoning.

Use a credible same-stage prevention competitor and a later decision that earlier feedback does not already supply.

title: Duration of cancer-surgery prophylaxis

fairness: About four weeks is a plausible best total course for this major cancer operation with persistent mobility limitation. No confident clinical contradiction identified offline.
The prevention-versus-treatment distinction and total-course framing are appropriate. The discharge progression follows the prior bleeding and prophylaxis decisions coherently.
Earlier feedback does not teach the duration, but the current update does; the duration recall does not earn two consequential steps.
suggestions: Replace the answer-bearing four-week reference with a neutral postoperative time point.
Require application of the risk and recovery findings to a supported discharge course; keep precise durations tied to verified evidence.

suggestions: Fix the unexplained second sheet. Seek acceptance for focused medication-calendar recall or redesign around an actual exposure/timing decision.
Do not invent a competing urgency or unsupported interval merely to raise difficulty.

title: Postoperative ketone-associated acidosis
clarityIssues: The task requests a medication-associated complication, but hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state is not phrased as medication-associated like the other choices.

The task is classic pattern recognition with one-line exclusions, not interpretation followed by a consequential decision.
Historical admission framing is coherent; later recovery data were not used to judge this first node.
suggestions: Use a neutral metabolic-complication task and same-category options.
Test a consequential action after interpreting the pattern, or compare genuinely plausible causes with adequate differentiating observations. Preserve the euglycemic safety lesson.

title: Empagliflozin during incomplete oral recovery
clarityIssues: 'Resume ... with the next retained meal' is conditional future advice, whereas the key describes what to do now. Readers may interpret it as waiting for recovery rather than restarting immediately.

cues.why: Only the key repeats the salient problem as an explanation.

After ketoacidosis associated with SGLT2 therapy, re-exposure requires assessment of the episode and contributors. This review does not approve automatic restart once meals resume.
Chronology is coherent and the first explanation does not give the restart rule, but the later item is an easy intolerance-to-hold match.

Separate current withholding from a future restart decision and obtain clinician review of any proposed post-ketoacidosis restart rule.

title: Awake gas exchange versus sleep testing
clarityIssues: 'Below the clinic reference band', 'above the laboratory interval' and 'marked obesity' conceal the degree of abnormality and do not establish severity or stability.

cues.why: Necessary awake physiology is contrasted with two overnight options; that contrast can narrow the answer independently of the chemistry interpretation.

fairness: ABG is a defensible priority with high suspicion for awake hypoventilation, while sleep testing addresses a related question. Both may be needed; the task does not sharply define the immediate unresolved problem.
The qualitative findings leave uncertainty about the intended pretest suspicion. This is a fairness concern, not a claim that ABG is wrong.
Potentially two consequential steps: integrate awake oxygenation/chemistry with sleep history, then select the investigation addressing the unresolved physiology. Standalone.
suggestions: Provide clinically reviewed constructed observations, ranges and relevant stability/context without inventing a cutoff.
Clarify the immediate abnormality to investigate while keeping the diagnosis and confirmatory test out of the lead-in. Ensure the competing sleep test is less appropriate for that specific question.

clarityIssues: The 'validated preoperative apnoea-risk report' is unnamed and merely 'flagged'; identify the instrument and reported result/limits.

cues.why: The absolute 'all' advertises an implausible blanket delay.

Compare concrete anesthesia/recovery plans at the same stage. Remove the absolute delay and rationale-bearing wrong option.

The later record follows preoperative decline coherently and can be solved from its update and shared context without the earlier answer. No particular facility eligibility or insurance entitlement is claimed.
suggestions: Retain the distinction between corridor walking, transfers and entrance steps. Keep the support recommendation functional rather than mandating a specific facility.

The separated task says only 'this prevention plan'; name delirium prevention.

Use balanced indication detail and credible medication competitors. Remove the key-specific absent-allergy qualifier unless necessary to distinguish a real competing indication.

title: New inattention with postvoid fullness
fairness: Bedside postvoid bladder assessment is the best immediate investigation given small voids, postvoid fullness and recent catheter removal. Neurologic testing is less immediately explanatory without focal findings or a more specific seizure pattern.

The resident must recognize acute fluctuating cognition and interpret apparent urine passage as compatible with retention, then prioritize a reversible contributor. The explanation appropriately avoids claiming a unique cause.

title: ART when enteral delivery is impossible
fairness: Coordinated temporary interruption of the complete regimen is the best offered approach during documented route failure after specialist/formulation review. Partial therapy is a credible error, and repeated dosing into returning drainage is unreliable.

The unavailable complete alternative is necessary to establish an unavoidable interval, not dispensable cueing. Interpreting delivery failure and applying a complete-regimen interruption principle provide two consequential steps.
No drug-specific substitution, restart rule or coinfection management is tested. No confident wrong key identified within this narrow scope.

Standalone and useful, but this specialized ART comparison is lower priority than commonly tested cardiac, VTE and delirium decisions. highYield=false reflects qualitative general-surgery scope judgment, not a verified exam-frequency claim.
suggestions: Retain specialist involvement and route-failure evidence. Give this lower coverage priority unless broader perioperative medication safety is an explicit owner objective.

This is uncertainty about the supplied discriminator, not a claim that mammography is the better answer. The present options mainly test simple modality selection.
First of two coherent nodes; its explanation does not disclose observation versus aspiration.
suggestions: State meaningful postoperative chronology and whether this is an early localized wound-site change.
Create a real target/acquisition decision or seek basic modality-selection acceptance. Do not use MRI as filler.

fairness: Urgent hand-surgical assessment is best for tense progressive swelling, sensory change and marked pain on passive extension after initial care. Continuing elevation without escalation is the meaningful wrong-stage competitor.
The resident distinguishes the progressive local injury from separate prior hives, then uses the trajectory to escalate beyond conservative measures. The warning signs are necessary safety data.

Antihistamine is weaker than serial local assessment as a distractor, but the latter remains credible. The key appropriately requests assessment rather than claiming a proven syndrome or mandatory operation.

fairness: Retaining the documented reaction and seeking drug-allergy expertise is best. Delayed blistering, mucosal involvement and organ injury make routine immediate-allergy testing/challenge pathways inappropriate.

Two consequential steps remain: recover the severe delayed phenotype from a misleading short label, then recognize changed eligibility for common delabeling approaches. Skin testing followed by challenge is a credible resident trap.
The history need not be forced into a single named severe reaction to answer this safety question. The key does not select an antibiotic or challenge protocol.

suggestions: Keep timing, mucosal findings and organ involvement. Do not extrapolate universal beta-lactam permissions or exclusions beyond the specialist-evaluation decision.

fairness: Clinical assessment without additional ischemia testing is best for the stated superficial local procedure without an independent cardiac indication.

Standalone; the explanation appropriately confines the conclusion to the represented absence of an independent testing indication.

title: Lisinopril before rescheduled surgery in HFrEF
clarityIssues: 'For the preoperative interval' does not distinguish a short omission from prolonged withdrawal; these are materially different plans.

cues.why: Calling the competing instruction generic prelabels it as less applicable.

cues.why: Only the key explicitly includes team coordination, giving it a cautious/comprehensive advantage.

cues.why: No supplied reason supports escalation in a stable patient; this is a weak third choice.

fairness: The explanation calls continuation 'reasonable', which does not establish that a brief preoperative omission is always wrong. Hypotension considerations and the actual interval could leave omission defensible.
This is a clinical fairness uncertainty, not a confident claim that continuation is inaccurate. The exact exclusive ranking requires clinician adjudication.

Two potentially meaningful steps are present: infer compensation from response and distinguish HFrEF therapy from hypertension-only instructions. The later node follows coherently and supplies its new diagnosis and recovery data independently.
suggestions: Define the omission interval and decision context, then have Melissa adjudicate whether continuation is uniquely best.
Use parallel coordination language, remove the editorial 'generic' cue, and replace unjustified escalation.
If both continuation and short omission remain acceptable, change the tested objective rather than making a permissive recommendation mandatory.

title: Valve assessment before major elective surgery
fairness: Concordant valve measurements with exertional presyncope support symptomatic severe aortic stenosis. Valve-team assessment before the nonurgent major operation is best.
Preserved EF does not resolve valve risk. Dobutamine testing is a plausible misapplication of another stenosis-evaluation pathway; surveillance overlooks the symptomatic context.
The learner interprets severity/symptoms rather than EF alone, then applies that interpretation to operative timing. No diagnosis label or decisive wording-only shortcut precedes the choice.
Standalone and high-yield. No confident clinical error identified; assessment is appropriately keyed instead of a mandatory valve procedure.
suggestions: Retain concordant measurements, exertional symptom and nonurgent context. Avoid an automatic procedure recommendation.

Compare credible preparation plans in a supported scenario where interpretation changes action, or seek basic-safety acceptance. Do not use antiemetic-only management to manufacture difficulty.
